01CLL798D / CHL7903 · Network SciencePrelim review · 09 Sep 2026

Minimum spanning trees
don't survive contact
with a hillside

Graph-theoretic topology optimisation of district-heating pipe networks — on two real German networks, real SRTM terrain, and a transport-phenomena cost model. We reproduce Gao et al. (2020), show its published results are not internally consistent, and rebuild the problem with terrain, hydraulic feasibility and reliability in the objective.

Q1

Is minimum length the same as minimum cost?

Q2

Is the cost-optimal tree even buildable?

Q3

What does fault tolerance cost?

Pathway 1 — reproduce & extend AixDHN · NASA SRTM 30 m · EN 253 · Eurostat Kruskal · Prim · Steiner · Laplacian spectral bisection
02The problemGraph formulation

A pipe network is a graph, and the topology is the design decision

V  =  1 plant + n consumer substations
E  =  every feasible trench route, w(e) = construction cost
feasible layout  =  connected, loop-free → spanning tree, |E| = V − 1
number of spanning trees  =  VV−2  (Cayley)

For our 41-node networks that is 4139 ≈ 1062 candidate layouts. Enumeration is hopeless, so the design is delegated to a greedy algorithm with a proof of optimality — provided the edge weight actually encodes cost.

The gap this project attacks

An MST is provably optimal for the weight you give it. Gao et al. give it straight-line distance. On real ground, distance is not cost, minimum length is not minimum cost, and the optimal tree may not even be hydraulically buildable.

Correction to our own abstract

The abstract said AixDHN would supply node/coordinate data for a pipe network. It does not — it has no pipes, no diameters, no per-node demand, only district polygons, aggregate demand and census cells. We verified this against the repository before use and built the node set ourselves by clustering the real cells.

04The networksResult

Two real networks, three topologies, one terrain model

Read the star column

The star is 3× the pipe length and 65 % more expensive per MWh — but it is the most reliable topology, losing only the largest single customer to any one failure. That trade-off is the whole subject of this project.

05Physics engineTransport phenomena

Momentum, heat and mass — and how each reaches back into the graph

Momentum

Darcy–Weisbach with Colebrook friction; discrete EN 253 sizing on velocity and 100 Pa/m specific drop. In a closed loop the static head cancels — pumping is friction only. Getting that wrong overstates hilly pumping by orders of magnitude.

Heat

Buried twin-pipe resistance Rself + Rmutual; the warm supply pipe shields the return, reducing total loss. DN300 at 110/50 °C loses 64.4 W per trench metre.

Mass

O₂ transport to the wall (Linton–Sherwood) sets corrosion, which sets failure rate. km ∝ u0.83D−0.17, so narrow fast branches corrode faster — topology changes reliability.

06ValidationDoes our physics agree with theirs?

We re-derived the paper's own heat-transfer coefficient from first principles

Gao et al.'s Table 1 prints λ and ε with swapped units. Rather than assume the swap, we computed ε independently: Churchill–Bernstein cross-flow over a 1 m cylinder at the paper's own wind speed v = 3.50 m/s, plus radiation from galvanised cladding.

hconvection  =  10.228 W·m−2K−1
hradiation   =   1.383
htotal      =  11.611
published    =  11.630
0.16 % error

An independent correlation lands within 0.16 % of the published value. That both validates our thermal model and proves the Table 1 units are swapped — without ever assuming it.

Other checks that passed

  • ρ = 0.60 kg/m³ → saturated steam near 1 atm → T ≈ 100 °C, matching "only low-pressure steam is considered"
  • Back-calculated MST heat loss 121 W/m — normal for an insulated steam main
  • Kruskal, heap-Prim, dense-Prim and NetworkX all return identical tree weight
  • O(V) tree flow solver matches the Eq(7)–(12) LP to 5×10−5

Insulation scaling, taken from the standard

Log–log fit over 22 real EN 253 catalogue sizes:

tins = 0.1025 · Dsteel0.391   (R = 0.963)

Real standards insulate sub-proportionally. The exponent comes from the standard, not from the data we validate against.

07ReproductionGao et al. (2020)

The MST column fits exactly. The held-out Star column does not.

Inverse reconstruction

The paper publishes no coordinates. We searched n and layout to match both published lengths at once:

n = 33 users, 2.99 km site
star  36,500.0 m  (−0.00 %)
MST   11,900.4 m  (+0.00 %)
ratio 3.067  (paper 3.067)

Calibrated: 87.5 kg/s steam, 167.6 mm insulation, ζelbow = 0.598 — all physically plausible.

Finding — Table 2 is not self-consistent

The published Star pipe cost (0.869) is lower than the MST (1.03) despite 3.07× the length. Under the paper's own Eq(13)–(14) that ratio requires a total demand of 357 kg/s, but the absolute MST cost requires 87.5 kg/s — a 3× contradiction.

Finding — the ESMT sits at a proved bound

Du & Hwang's Steiner ratio theorem proves LSMT/LMST ≥ √3/2 = 0.86603 for any planar point set. The paper reports 1.03/1.19 = 0.86555. Within table rounding, but at the very edge of geometric possibility.

08Result 1Terrain-weighted routing

A longer tree can be the cheaper tree

Stuttgart — hilly −3.0 %total annual cost, for a tree that is 0.03 km longer. 23.09 → 22.39 EUR/MWh.
Bremen — flat 0.0 %terrain weighting returns the identical tree. The control experiment behaves exactly as it must.
Why this matters

Minimising length and minimising cost are the same problem only on flat ground. The saving is modest but it is free — same algorithm, better weight.

09Result 2Hydraulic feasibility

In Stuttgart the cost-optimal tree cannot legally be built

p(z) = pref + ρg(zref − z)

required at high point  psat+margin = 1.93 bar
static over 282 m   ρgΔz = 26.3 bar
pipe class             PN16 = 16 bar
single-zone relief limit = 151 m
The constraint terrain really imposes

Not pumping cost — pressure class. One zone can hold 151 m of relief. Stuttgart has 282 m, so a single-zone network is infeasible and the design needs 2 pressure zones with an exchanger station between them. Bremen needs 1.

Spectral bisection doing real engineering

Choosing where to split is a balanced minimum-cut problem: separate nodes by elevation while cutting as few pipes as possible, because every cut pipe needs a heat-exchanger station. The Fiedler vector of the Laplacian is the classical relaxation of exactly that — the course's spectral bisection used as a hydraulic design tool.

Every tree edge is a bridge — and Steiner trees make it worse

Answering the fault-propagation question

A Steiner tree is still a tree. Adding Steiner points buys length — RSMT is the cheapest topology at 20.87 EUR/MWh — but it concentrates flow into shared trunks, so it is more fragile, not less. Steiner solves cost; only cycles solve faults.

Expected Unserved Demand

EUD = Σe λe × MTTR × Dstranded(e), with λe from real DH failure statistics, scaled per branch by our own O₂-corrosion model. Topology → velocity → corrosion → failure rate.

13AlgorithmsKruskal vs Prim, implemented from scratch

The textbook prediction is wrong for this graph

At V = 1600  (E = 1,279,200)

ImplementationRuntimeα
Kruskal — union–find420 ms 2.08
Prim — binary heap6114 ms 2.52
Prim — dense array 28.8 ms 1.09
Correction to our own prelim slides

We predicted density would favour Prim. It favours the dense array Prim — 212× faster than the heap version and 15× faster than Kruskal. Heap-Prim is the worst choice here: it pushes O(E) entries through a priority queue. Kruskal beats it by terminating early, examining only 0.7 % of the sorted edge list.

Asymptotic order alone does not pick the algorithm. Graph density and implementation constants decide it — which is exactly the kind of claim a benchmark, not a textbook, has to settle.

14SummaryCost breakdown

Where the money actually goes

Capital dominates

Trench cost is 80–90 % of TAC. That is why topology — which sets how many metres you dig — is the dominant design decision, and why the MST framing is right even when its weight is wrong.

Pumping is small

Because the static head cancels round a closed loop. A model that adds ρgΔz to the pump duty would overstate hilly pumping by three orders of magnitude.

Zones are not small

Stuttgart's second pressure zone is a real annualised cost that no length-based objective can see. It appears only when terrain enters the constraint set.

The thesis in one line

On flat ground a minimum spanning tree is the right answer. On real terrain it is neither minimum-cost nor necessarily buildable — and because every tree edge is a bridge, it is never robust. Terrain belongs in the weight, pressure class belongs in the constraints, and reliability belongs in the objective.
